## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
On the first Tuesday of every month, the library put its broken things on a table by the front door. Anyone could take one, provided they wrote down what they intended to do with it. Most people were honest. Beside a lamp with no cord, someone had written *Learn about lamps*. Beside a wooden duck with no head: *Make this worse*.

Nina took a clock that gained eleven minutes every hour. Under *Intended Use*, she wrote *Kitchen*. The librarian, who had been watching her over the rims of her glasses, said, “That’s a place.”

“It’s where I intend to use it.”

“Fair enough.”

The clock was yellow and had a second hand that moved with the earnest, slightly panicked energy of a person carrying soup through a crowded room. Nina hung it above the stove. It was three in the afternoon, and by dinner it would be nearly bedtime.

She had recently inherited the house from her father, who had kept a clock in every room, all set to different times. He claimed this was because he didn’t believe an hour should be allowed to arrive everywhere at once. In fact, he had never bothered to learn how to set any of them. For six years the microwave had read 0:00. When Nina was a teenager and came home late, he would consult the microwave and say, “Midnight exactly,” which meant she was in just enough trouble for him to put the kettle on.

The house had come with everything in it, including a dining table that rocked and a jar of screws whose original purposes could no longer be determined. Her father had saved the screws on the theory that whenever you threw one away, its purpose immediately revealed itself. Nina opened the jar, chose a short brass screw, and used it to hang the yellow clock. This was the first convincing evidence she had ever encountered in support of his theory.

At five thirty the following morning, someone knocked on the back door. It was her neighbor, Mrs. Vale, holding a casserole dish with a blue lid.

“I saw your kitchen light,” Mrs. Vale said.

Nina had left it on all night. She used to do the same thing when her father was alive and she went out somewhere he disapproved of. This allowed him to pretend he had fallen asleep in the chair by accident.

“What’s in the dish?” Nina asked.

“Nothing. I thought I’d start returning things before I forgot who they belonged to.”

It wasn’t Nina’s dish. She recognized it as the one Mrs. Vale had carried into the house a week after the funeral, full of baked apples. Her father had hated baked apples. He said they were what happened when you gave up halfway through a pie. Nina had eaten them cold, standing at the counter, and had washed the dish twice because washing it was the only task she could think of that had a definite end.

She said, “Do you want coffee?”

While the kettle heated, Mrs. Vale looked up at the clock. The hour hand was halfway to nine.

“Goodness,” she said, and sat down.

They drank two cups. Mrs. Vale told Nina that the man who had been delivering her newspaper for years had quit and that she had never learned his name. She knew he had a daughter in Ohio and that he couldn’t eat peaches. He had once shown her a photograph of a retaining wall he’d built. “I kept thinking it would be embarrassing to ask,” she said. “And then every year it got more embarrassing.”

“Call the newspaper.”

“And say what?”

“That you liked the wall.”

Mrs. Vale considered this. “I did like the wall. It wasn’t fancy, but you could see he’d thought about the water.”

When she left, she took the dish with her. Nina watched her cross the yard, balancing it flat in both hands as if it were full.

On the next first Tuesday, Nina carried the clock back to the library. The librarian lifted it to her ear, then looked at the face.

“Didn’t work out in the kitchen?”

“It worked out fine,” Nina said. “I think I’d like someone else to have it.”

There was no space for that on the form, so the librarian handed her a blank card. Nina thought about writing a warning. Instead she wrote *Gains eleven minutes an hour. Easy to hang.* She set the clock down between a sewing machine and a pair of binoculars through which everything appeared slightly green.

A boy in a red coat picked it up before she had reached the door. His grandmother, who seemed to have come in for the sewing machine, read the card aloud.

“Is that a lot?” he asked.

His grandmother counted silently, tapping one finger against her coat. “It’ll get about four and a half hours ahead every day.”

“Can it get a whole day ahead?”

“I suppose it can.”

The boy stood very still. “But how will you know when it does?”

His grandmother looked at the clock again. Then she looked up at the librarian, who shrugged. The boy tucked it under his arm and went over to the form.

Nina didn’t stay to see what he wrote. She went home and pulled the dining table away from the wall. The short leg had been shimmed with a piece of folded cardboard that had flattened over the years. She sat on the floor and unfolded it. It was the back of a packet of sunflower seeds. On the front, beneath a picture of three improbably tall flowers, someone had written a telephone number in pencil.

She called it. A woman answered, and Nina explained where she had found the number.

“Oh,” the woman said. “Did they ever come up?”

Nina remembered them then. Her father had planted them beneath the eaves, where there was hardly any sun. Only one had grown tall enough to reach the corner of the kitchen window. Whenever Nina did the dishes, she’d had to lean a little to the left to see its face.

“One did,” she said.

“Well,” the woman said, with the satisfaction of someone whose arithmetic had worked out, “that’s all he asked for.”
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story uses recurring household objects and understated dialogue to carry a grief narrative.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gently wry and attentive to the emotional lives of ordinary things: a fast clock, a returned casserole dish, a jar of screws, a flattened seed packet. Nina’s grief appears through habits and small tasks rather than direct explanation, while her father’s eccentricities remain affectionate without being sentimentalized. The story invites the reader to notice how objects preserve unfinished connections—and how a modest gesture, like telling a stranger you liked his wall, can help someone begin one.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds clocks and broken or repurposed household objects as measures of time, memory, and care. It pairs private bereavement with small acts of neighborly attention, and lets inherited habits pass into new hands rather than resolving grief through a grand revelation. Its humor is mild and humane, as in the father’s many badly set clocks and the boy’s question about whether one can get a whole day ahead.

## Evidence line
> The clock was yellow and had a second hand that moved with the earnest, slightly panicked energy of a person carrying soup through a crowded room.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story is coherent and stylistically distinctive, with recurring objects and understated humor repeatedly serving its themes of grief, time, and ordinary kindness.
